react_result.final_narrative_text: The differentially abundant metabolites converge overwhelmingly on tryptophan metabolism (KEGG:hsa00380), which achieved rank 1 in all three independent paradigms tested: RaMP multi-database ORA (FDR = 5.56 × 10⁻¹⁸, fold enrichment 778×), MetaboAnalystR KEGG-specific PSEA (p = 1.59 × 10⁻⁸, 6 of 10 input compounds mapped), and Mummichog m/z-direct network analysis (p = 0.0019, 17 of 18 pathway compounds matched). This represents a genuine cross-paradigm consensus rather than a single-tool artefact. Seven metabolites from the input list — L-tryptophan, serotonin, melatonin, tryptamine, indoleacetaldehyde, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, and quinolinic acid — are direct members of the KEGG:hsa00380 roster. A secondary signal in Mummichog identified arginine and proline metabolism (p = 0.027), anchored by 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylic acid (C03912) and its hydroxylated analogue pyrroline hydroxycarboxylic acid (C04281), both of which are also structurally validated intermediates in proline biosynthesis and glutamate flux. The IDO metabolic pathway (WP:WP5414, FDR = 1.36 × 10⁻⁸) captures the kynurenine-branch intermediates (quinolinic acid and 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid), indicating that not only the canonical serotonin/melatonin arm of tryptophan catabolism is perturbed, but also the neurotoxic kynurenine shunt that feeds NAD⁺ biosynthesis. Serotonin and melatonin biosynthesis (REACT:R-HSA-209931, FDR = 3.38 × 10⁻⁸) corroborates the three most recognized downstream effectors of tryptophan — tryptophan itself, serotonin, and melatonin — as the primary driver metabolites. L-valine, while present in the input, maps weakly and appears as a singlet in branched-chain amino acid metabolism (KEGG:hsa00290, p = 0.044), representing a secondary signal of lower confidence than the tryptophan-axis findings. The biological interpretation is that the treatment strongly dysregulates tryptophan catabolism across both its neurotransmitter (serotonin/melatonin) and immune/kynurenine branches, with potential downstream consequences for neurobehavioral function and NAD⁺-dependent cellular energetics.

Seven metabolites from the input list — L-tryptophan, serotonin, melatonin, tryptamine, indoleacetaldehyde, 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid, and quinolinic acid — are direct members of the KEGG:hsa00380 roster. A secondary signal in Mummichog identified arginine and proline metabolism (p = 0.027), anchored by 1-pyrroline-5-carboxylic acid (C03912) and its hydroxylated analogue pyrroline hydroxycarboxylic acid (C04281), both of which are also structurally validated intermediates in proline biosynthesis and glutamate flux. The IDO metabolic pathway (WP:WP5414, FDR = 1.36 × 10⁻⁸) captures the kynurenine-branch intermediates (quinolinic acid and 3-hydroxyanthranilic acid), indicating that not only the canonical serotonin/melatonin arm of tryptophan catabolism is perturbed, but also the neurotoxic kynurenine shunt that feeds NAD⁺ biosynthesis. Serotonin and melatonin biosynthesis (REACT:R-HSA-209931, FDR = 3.38 × 10⁻⁸) corroborates the three most recognized downstream effectors of tryptophan — tryptophan itself, serotonin, and melatonin — as the primary driver metabolites. L-valine, while present in the input, maps weakly and appears as a singlet in branched-chain amino acid metabolism (KEGG:hsa00290, p = 0.044), representing a secondary signal of lower confidence than the tryptophan-axis findings. The biological interpretation is that the treatment strongly dysregulates tryptophan catabolism across both its neurotransmitter (serotonin/melatonin) and immune/kynurenine branches, with potential downstream consequences for neurobehavioral function and NAD⁺-dependent cellular energetics.
